name: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, Lord Thurlow
bio: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, 2nd Baron Thurlow (1781–1829), was an English poet and nephew of the Lord Chancellor of the same title. He published several volumes of verse in the 1810s and 1820s.
His lyric "May" is printed in The Oxford Book of English Verse.

poems.title: May
poems.author: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, Lord Thurlow
poems.collection: The Oxford Book of English Verse (1900)
poems.text:
May! queen of blossoms,
  And fulfilling flowers,
With what pretty music
  Shall we charm the hours?
Wilt thou have pipe and reed,
Blown in the open mead?
Or to the lute give heed
  In the green bowers?

Thou hast no need of us,
  Or pipe or wire;
Thou hast the golden bee
  Ripen’d with fire;
And many thousand more
Songsters, that thee adore,
Filling earth’s grassy floor
  With new desire.

Thou hast thy mighty herds,
  Tame and free-livers;
Doubt not, thy music too
  In the deep rivers;
And the whole plumy flight
Warbling the day and night--
Up at the gates of light,
  See, the lark quivers!

poems.title: To a Bird, that haunted the Waters of Laaken, in the Winter
poems.author: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, Lord Thurlow
poems.collection: A New Library of Poetry and Song, ed. William Cullen Bryant (1877)
poems.text:
O melancholy Bird, a winter's day
Thou standest by the margin of the pool,
And, taught by God, dost thy whole being school
To patience, which all evil can allay:
God has appointed thee the fish thy prey,
And given thyself a lesson to the fool
Unthrifty, to submit to moral rule,
And his unthinking course by thee to weigh.
There need not schools nor the professor's chair,
Though these be good, true wisdom to impart:
He who has not enough for these to spare
Of time or gold, may yet amend his heart,
And teach his soul by brooks and rivers fair:
Nature is always wise in every part.

poems.title: When in the woods I wander all alone
poems.author: Edward Hovell-Thurlow, Lord Thurlow
poems.collection: The Home Book of Verse, ed. Burton Egbert Stevenson (1918)
poems.text:
When in the woods I wander all alone,
The woods that are my solace and delight,
Which I more covet than a prince's throne,
My toil by day and canopy by night;
(Light heart, light foot, light food, and slumber light,
These lights shall light us to old age's gate,
While monarchs, whom rebellious dreams affright,
Heavy with fear, death's fearful summons wait;)
Whilst here I wander, pleased to be alone,
Weighing in thought the world's no-happiness,
I cannot choose but wonder at its moan,
Since so plain joys the woody life can bless:
Then live who may where honied words prevail,
I with the deer, and with the nightingale!
